Uber bad idea

By: Anina Peens | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We investigate how fake Uber drivers trap young women at airports

Unique Selling Point:
After a young woman took an Uber from OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg, she was never seen again. A couple of days later, her remains were discovered in the Vaal river. We investigate whether a fake uber syndicate may be targeting young women at airports.

Summary:
Fake Uber drivers are rife at the country’s airports. They wait at the arrivals sections of airports holding up boards indicating that they are drivers for Uber. They are believed to target single travelers, especially young women who may appear not to be travelwise. When the Uber is ordered, fake drivers walk up to their targets and inform that they are the driver that have been hailed/ordered.
Unsuspecting victims follow them to their cars and once they are in the car, they cannot get out. When the real Uber drivers who were ordered arrive to pick up the person, it is too late. The fake Uber driver then informs his passenger/target that the other Uber driver is only calling because business is tight, and they fight for passengers. They tell their victims to ignore the calls of the other Uber drivers or to block their numbers. Once they are outside the airport, they spin off and it is only then victims realize, they are being kidnapped. In some cases, the victims are robbed and dropped off next to the road, but in more serious cases, female victims are raped and sometimes killed.


Further information:
Uber Bad Idea

On 26 April, thirty-five-year-old Yolande Botes was reported missing. According to her family, Botes traveled from George to Johannesburg to visit her children. She arrived at OR Tambo International airport on the same day she was reported missing. She is believed to have taken an Uber at her arrival. She was never seen again.

Fake Uber drivers are rife at the country’s airports. They wait at the arrivals sections of airports holding up boards indicating that they are drivers for Uber. They are believed to target single travelers, especially young women who may appear not to be travelwise. When the Uber is ordered, fake drivers walk up to their targets and inform that they are the driver that have been hailed/ordered.
Unsuspecting victims follow them to their cars and once they are in the car, they cannot get out. When the real Uber drivers who were ordered arrive to pick up the person, it is too late. The fake Uber driver then informs his passenger/target that the other Uber driver is only calling because business is tight, and they fight for passengers. They tell their victims to ignore the calls of the other Uber drivers or to block their numbers. Once they are outside the airport, they spin off and it is only then victims realize, they are being kidnapped. In some cases, the victims are robbed and dropped off next to the road, but in more serious cases, female victims are raped and sometimes killed.

Although circumstances surrounding the death of Yolandi Botes may be different, the fact that she disappeared after taking an Uber, paved the way to spread awareness about fake Uber drivers and the tell-tale signs to look out for, especially for people who are not seasonal travelers.

The case of Botes:

On 7 May, fishermen found body parts drifting down the Vaal river. The body parts were later identified as that of Yolandi Botes. She was chopped up by her killers who may or may not have been the kidnappers.

Shortly after Botes disappeared, a hotel owner in Kempton Park discovered a bedroom in his hotel, filled with blood stains. A knife was found underneath the bed. The person who checked in to the room had left no telephone number or Identity document and checked out of the hotel around 3am in the morning. Could this be the same location where Botes has been chopped up? And could this be connected to the fake Uber syndicates?

WYNAND agreed to one return flight for the case study to JHB

Reason for legal: Allegations of a lack of security measured by Uber may be made to which they will have to reply. ACSA had a right of reply as to allegations made that they are not providing proper security at the airports to protect passengers

Press Release:


Masa Kekana: “Being bombarded at the airport by multiple drivers is slightly intimidating, especially as a woman travelling alone. While there's nothing wrong with taxi service drivers trying to get passengers, beware if they urge you to not use the official app.”



Rideshare Roulette

Legislation is pending at the federal level in the United States after a young woman was kidnapped and killed in 2019. The prominent case of Samantha Josephson (21), who had ordered an Uber but then got into a different car where the driver allegedly used childproof locks to prevent her from escaping, led to proposed legislation to improve protection for drivers and passengers. In South Africa, in April, Yolandi Botes (34) took a cab from the airport and was never seen again. Carte Blanche tracks the experiences of unsuspecting young women who mistakenly followed imposters posing as cab drivers but, once in the car, realised the danger.

Producer: Anina Peens | Presenter: Masa Kekana

Watch the trailer

Script:



Riding Roulette

INTRO
VO
There’s a variety of e-hailing taxi and cab services on the market for passengers to choose from. But when app-based systems are bypassed, it opens up opportunities for criminals to enter the system.
The murder of Yolandi Botes in April, whose body was found in the Vaalriver sent shockwaves through the country. Shortly before her murder, she traveled from George to OR Tambo airport in Johannesburg.

LINK
“Getting into the wrong cab can be very dangerous. Yolandi Botes was reported missing after taking a cab from the OR Tambo international airport in April. Although Uber says the driver completed his trip, the incident flung bogus drivers into the spotlight and the safety and risks of cab-hailing services”

VO
Megan Davies says, she still has nightmares about being kidnapped, as she was misled at the OR Tambo airport, by a bogus driver.
Coming from a small farming town in the Northern Cape, Megan had never used an e-hailing service before. She says she was lucky enough to escape what she believes was an attempted kidnapping.

SUPER@ MEGAN, NO SUPER MOV 14470031
20’19’28’24
it freaks me out it does because it could have gone horribly wrong. Just due to the fact that you are naïve, and you believe, you trust, it gets taken advantage of”

VO
When ordering an Uber, you enter your destination into the app, wait for an assigned driver and check that the driver and car detail match information given on the app. But Megan did not know this. When she arrived at OR Tambo airport, Megan downloaded the Uber app, ordered a ride and waited at the general pickup point.

SUPER@ MEGAN NO STRAP
“Somebody approached me and said, are you the lady who just summonsed a taxi? And I said yes, I am, and it was way quicker than what they said …

USE REENACTMENTS
“So, I took my bag and I put it in the backseat of the car, and I got in in front”
“He asked me specifically, what address am I taking you to?”
MASA: Even though you had put the address in your Uber app?”
“Yes, I thought it was just a confirmation”

VO
As they were exiting the airport, the actual Uber she HAD ordered via the app, arrived and phoned her. She told THE DRIVER she HAD TAKEN another Uber. He told her that WAS NOT THE correct procedure and that the ordered ride should be cancelled in the app. The driver OF THE CAR she HAD TAKEN NOW told her to ignore the real Uber driver.

SUPER@ MEGAN NO STRAP
“The driver said just ignore your phone the next time it rings, it’s just professional jealousy

VO
But the Uber driver kept on calling.

SUPER@ MEGAN NO STRAP
“My phone just kept on ringing and I picked up the phone and I said, you know what please and the person did not even give me a chance, he just said, you don’t have to come with me, just get out of the car that you are in now, because they are busy kidnapping you”

VO
Megan realized she may be in real danger and told the driver to stop – but he refused.

SUPER@ MEGAN NO STRAP
“I tried to open the door but it would not open. And I thought, child lock maybe? And I said, please open the door, I am getting out here. If you don’t open the door, I will go as far as to kick out your window and it cause commotion, so just stop… and I opened the door and I got out, while the car was driving.

VO
As she got out of the vehicle, she caught a glimpse of the driver’s phone.

SUPER@ MEGAN NO STRAP
“…it was definitely WhatsApp and there was a picture of me while I was waiting with my bag and trolley. He sent a voice note but still in a language that I couldn’t understand.

VO
Megan has reason to believe that her ordeal may have been a kidnapping. Crime trends and statistics analyst for the Institute of Security Studies, Lizette Lancaster says, robbery has increased significantly during the last year and kidnappings often happen with the intention to rob victims.

SUPER@LIZETTE LANCASTER: INSTITUTE FOR SECURITY STUDIES
“A lot of people that are hijacked or in this case picked up from the street or a place where they are waiting, and they are driven around to get access to their ATM cards and such.”

VO
The 2019 to 2020 statistics show a 16% increase in kidnappings in South Africa with 6623 cases reported. The ISS crime hub compared general kidnapping trends to what happened to Megan.

SUPER@LIZETTE LANCASTER: INSTITUTE FOR SECURITY STUDIES
“Looking at the circumstances in this case, it could be a number of things ranging from the normal sort of extortion type racket where people are held but they are very small numbers. The most likely scenario would have been a robbery that was planned. Or simply an Uber driver that was trying to undercut the regular business”

VO
At OR Tambo international airport, drivers posing as Uber drivers, crowd the exit doors. We went undercover to see how they operate. Watch as various drivers approach in a short period.

UBER 1 AUDIO
2’40”
“Uber ride mam? Uber? “Yes mam” Are you an Uber? “Yes mam” I just ordered an Uber “How far is it?” Mmm 8 minutes “See I am right here
UBER 2 AUDIO
“Uber, you want Uber?” I am waiting for my Uber. “But talk to me I can take you. We can kill the middleman and talk to me. All of us here we are Uber drivers waiting for clients”

VO
These drivers follow and hustle travelers to take rides with them for cheaper prices than what Uber is charging.

UPSOUND
Uber driver: Uber takes 30% of our money….

LINK
“a Registered Uber driver is most likely not going to stand outside airport doors with a sign written, Uber, airports have designated parking zones for taxis and shuttles. So, the guy stopping you as you get out of the airport claiming to be Uber drivers, are more often than not, not actual Uber drivers”

VO
General manager for Uber Southern Africa, Frans Hiemstra says the problem with fake Ubers drivers at the country’s airports has been coming for years.

SUPER@ FRANS HIEMSTRA: UBER: SOUTHERN AFRICA
1’57”
The important thing is that an uber ride can only be requested through the app so no matter in what hurry you are, the person harassing you outside the baggage claim is not your actual Uber driver…

VO
Experts say bypassing the e-hailing system paves the way for kidnapping and other crimes. But it doesn’t end there. Bogus drivers are sometimes in cahoots with registered drivers. Private investigator Wendy Pascoe, scrutinized the phenomenon of app sharing.

SUPER@ WENDY PASCOE: PRIVATE INVESTIGATOR
“What they do is they rent out their services to somebody else with the vehicle.
If you have to make 2000 for the week, you do your bit then you rent it to your friend or whoever else is going to rent it from you then they can make up the money you need to make for the week. So you can rent out the app.”

VO
Pascoe adds, that as in the case with Megan’s foreign driver, criminals enter the system when apps are rented to undocumented foreigners.

SUPER@ WENDY PASCOE: PRIVATE INVESTIGATOR
“Either they not legally here or have legal documentation to present so it is easier to just rent than to go through the actual channels of producing an ID and filling out the forms because that will declined”

VO
Uber says it is adapting safety technology on the app to curb this transgression.

VO
SUPER@ FRANS HIEMSTRA: UBER: SOUTHERN AFRICA
“We do have a zero-tolerance policy to it and it is actually very clearly in violation with our community safety guidelines. The reality is that we have put a lot of technology in place to mitigate for this. So, the first one is real time ID check where drivers will periodically be prompted to take a selfie and we have sophisticated facial recognition technology that then matches the driver’s picture to the picture we have on record and the drivers national ID.”

VO
Uber says it has been reaching out to Airports companies South Africa to assist them in removing the fake drivers. ACSA is the managing body of all airports in the country.

SUPER@ FRANS HIEMSTRA: UBER: SOUTHERN AFRICA
“I do think it is important specifically at airports for some physical intervention and I think a lot of the work can be done by ACSA. Those touters need to be removed;

MASA
“You say you have a good relationship with ACSA, but they don’t seem to get a hold of this, these guys are not being removed”
SUPER@ FRANS HIEMSTRA: UBER: SOUTHERN AFRICA
“We have really done our part to push ACSA to do this, I think the next step is up to them to remove these touters. This has actually been going on for quite some time as many airport users have seen and I am really looking forward to ACSA acting and removing these people.

VO
ACSA says airport law enforcement cannot investigate complaints without witness statements.
LINK
“In a written reply Airport companies South Africa, or ACSA says if there are any human traffickers or kidnappers operating from the airports, they would only investigate if people who have fallen victim to the crimes or narrowly escaped, come forward and that, these incidents would have to be reported to the police first”
VO
While the problem remains the responsibility of the authorities, it is up to passengers to take precaution when hailing e-cabs.
SUPER@ WENDY PASCOE: PRIVATE INVESTIGATOR
Conversation with Masa at the Uber car about safety…




PROMOS
“It is never a good idea to get into a car with a stranger. Yet bogus cab drivers offer cheaper rides than registered E-hailing services. Does this pave the way for crimes such as human trafficking? We investigate

PROMO 2
“The horrific killing of Yolandi Botes sent shockwaves through the country since she was last seen taking a cab at OR Tambo international airport, we shift the focus to bogus drivers, and the safety of cab-hailing services.

VO PROMOS
We go undercover to find out how cab hailing services are bypassed by bogus drivers claiming to represent registered service providers, especially at the country’s main airports.

Jumping into cab is sometimes an effective way of traveling. But what happens when you get into the wrong car? We take a look at fake drivers claiming to represent registered service providers.

What happens if you get into the wrong cab and you cannot get out? There was a 16% increase in kidnappings last year.
Are bogus cab drivers creating opportunities for criminals? We investigate.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We investigate how fake Uber drivers trap young women at airports
metadata.Unique Selling Point: After a young woman took an Uber from OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg, she was never seen again. A couple of days later, her remains were discovered in the Vaal river. We investigate whether a fake uber syndicate may be targeting young women at airports.
metadata.Summary: Fake Uber drivers are rife at the country’s airports. They wait at the arrivals sections of airports holding up boards indicating that they are drivers for Uber. They are believed to target single travelers, especially young women who may appear not to be travelwise. When the Uber is ordered, fake drivers walk up to their targets and inform that they are the driver that have been hailed/ordered. Unsuspecting victims follow them to their cars and once they are in the car, they cannot get out. When the real Uber drivers who were ordered arrive to pick up the person, it is too late. The fake Uber driver then informs his passenger/target that the other Uber driver is only calling because business is tight, and they fight for passengers. They tell their victims to ignore the calls of the other Uber drivers or to block their numbers. Once they are outside the airport, they spin off and it is only then victims realize, they are being kidnapped. In some cases, the victims are robbed and dropped off next to the road, but in more serious cases, female victims are raped and sometimes killed.
metadata.Further information: Uber Bad Idea On 26 April, thirty-five-year-old Yolande Botes was reported missing. According to her family, Botes traveled from George to Johannesburg to visit her children. She arrived at OR Tambo International airport on the same day she was reported missing. She is believed to have taken an Uber at her arrival. She was never seen again. Fake Uber drivers are rife at the country’s airports. They wait at the arrivals sections of airports holding up boards indicating that they are drivers for Uber. They are believed to target single travelers, especially young women who may appear not to be travelwise. When the Uber is ordered, fake drivers walk up to their targets and inform that they are the driver that have been hailed/ordered. Unsuspecting victims follow them to their cars and once they are in the car, they cannot get out. When the real Uber drivers who were ordered arrive to pick up the person, it is too late. The fake Uber driver then informs his passenger/target that the other Uber driver is only calling because business is tight, and they fight for passengers. They tell their victims to ignore the calls of the other Uber drivers or to block their numbers. Once they are outside the airport, they spin off and it is only then victims realize, they are being kidnapped. In some cases, the victims are robbed and dropped off next to the road, but in more serious cases, female victims are raped and sometimes killed. Although circumstances surrounding the death of Yolandi Botes may be different, the fact that she disappeared after taking an Uber, paved the way to spread awareness about fake Uber drivers and the tell-tale signs to look out for, especially for people who are not seasonal travelers. The case of Botes: On 7 May, fishermen found body parts drifting down the Vaal river. The body parts were later identified as that of Yolandi Botes. She was chopped up by her killers who may or may not have been the kidnappers. Shortly after Botes disappeared, a hotel owner in Kempton Park discovered a bedroom in his hotel, filled with blood stains. A knife was found underneath the bed. The person who checked in to the room had left no telephone number or Identity document and checked out of the hotel around 3am in the morning. Could this be the same location where Botes has been chopped up? And could this be connected to the fake Uber syndicates?
